Room (86): wall W with door to the rear service corridor; A large arched niche, with a black background, is located in the central panel, on the right there is an oblique niche, whose bottom is patent, with an obvious function of a window. The vignette of the central panel (gorgoneìon) was removed from the yellow plinth in the Bourbon era. The red middle area repeats the pattern already described in fig. 142.
150. Room (86): wall W, section N: detail of the small picture with a black background (hortus conclusus) of the middle area.
151. Room (89): mosaic floor of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, with a border of black and white bands and a marginal flounce of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp.

152. Room (89), N wall: red plinth; white middle area with panels outlined by edges of carpet with corollas and palmettes and supports, the side ones by metal jars and the central one by a crouching sphinx, separated by architectural glimpses crossed by plant candelabra with shoots.

153. Room (89), wall E: on the red plinth, the white middle area is divided into a side panel bordered by edges of a carpet with corollas and palmettes, supported by metal jars, surmounted by a square with marine thèasos between acroterial sirens, and a central vignette (cupid in flight). The central panel with a painting (which has disappeared) is limited at the bottom by a horizontal thyrsus supported by a crouching sphinx and at the top by a double-arched garland whose central motif was removed in the Bourbon era. They are separated by an architectural view crossed by a candelabra with shoots; a freio with metopes containing stylized gold marks the transition to the upper white area with a golden candelabrum surmounted by a globe and garland with hanging mask, in the center and candelabra with shoots on the side.
154. Room (89), wall E, section N. The detail of the painting allows us to grasp the engraved guide lines for the execution of the carpet edges. 77 N40503
155. Room (89), wall E, detail of the painting almost illegible.

156. Room (89), wall E: the central motif of the upper part of the panel consists of two birds facing each other on the disc of a short metal element under which the two garlands converge, joined by a cat mask. Above the metopes with flowers. The piece, now in the Museo Naz. of Naples (Inv. 9935) is mounted upside down in a pastiche in which two other fragments are gathered, with hanging situlas, probably coming from the courtyard (31).

157. Room (89): the S wall retains the upper area with a mystical cyst on a Delphic tripod and thyrsis crossed with acroterial swans, from which hang garlands with rhytòn and tfmpanon. The gaps are due to cuts from the Bourbon era.

158. Room (89): the central fragment of this architectural foreshortening crossed by a candelabrum with shoots certainly comes from the S wall, consisting of the assembly, in a single frame (Inv. 9856 of the Museo Naz. in Naples) of three non-contiguous fragments detached from the same room.

157. Room (89): the S wall retains the upper area with a mystical cyst on a Delphic tripod and thyrsis crossed with acroterial swans, from which hang garlands with rhytòn and tfmpanon. The gaps are due to cuts from the Bourbon era.

160. Room (89): the O wall repeated, as far as can be seen, the same scheme as the opposite E wall, but the details are more legible for the best state of preservation. The cartoon was removed in the Bourbon era.

161. Room (89): four fragments detached from this room are mounted in a single frame (Inv. 9611 of the National Museum of Naples). These are two vignettes described by Weber AnnInst 1830 as "seated woman with rose sleeping" and "naked man with leaning cane", coming from the middle area perhaps

162. Environment (90). The transition between the service area W of the portico and the actual domus was all uniformly decorated. On a high plinth in black and white imitation marble divided into panels, the white middle area with red squares is arranged.

163. Biclinio (91): very bright room due to the windows open to the N and E and the cold tone of the large blue surfaces. N wall with the red plinth divided into panels with plants; in the blue middle area, the panels, framed by carpet borders on red bands, with paintings removed in the Bourbon era, are separated by architectural views with a white background closed by red partitions; of the upper blue zone, only the lowest part remains.  77 N40509

164. Biclinio (91): wall E with a square window that interrupts the middle area, on which there is a rectangular window, closed by a sliding door. The compositional scheme is the same as on the N wall, but the side panels were devoid of paintings.

165. Biclinio (91), S wall: it is the only continuous wall in the room and the one that preserves the largest number of elements of the decorative structure, so much so that it has allowed the recognition of some pieces of the Museo Naz. of Naples. Red plinth divided into panels and compartments with plants. Blue middle area with a taut carpet in the centre, with a border of a carpet with running waves and side panels with edges of a trefoil carpet, separated by architectural views on a white background, closed by red partitions, from which, in the Bourbon era, the vignette was removed as well as the central painting and the foreshortening on the right. Upper blue area with painting.  77 N40508

166. Biclinio (91), S wall, section E: painting of the upper area, with a large red border decorated with stretched garlands. It depicts a marine thèasos of monsters and dolphins. The peculiarity of the whole has made it possible to recognize a fragment of the Naz. of Naples, almost completely vanished, which probably constituted the pendant of the latter.

167. Biclinio (91), S wall, O section: detached architectural view from the Bourbon era. The detail of the two different edges of the carpet on a red background, and a very small residue of the blue panel were the first clues from which the provenance of this piece was recognized (Inv. 9974 of the Museo Naz. in Naples).

168. Biclinio (91): probably from the W section of the S wall (or from the E section of the N wall) comes this fragment (now in the National Museum of Naples and without inventory number) very badly preserved, but clearly recognizable by a thèasos of sea monsters, in yellow monochrome on a white background within a large red border with garlands.

169. Biclinio (91), W wall with the door towards (93). A variant of the decorative motifs already described, within the same scheme, is the border of lotus and palmette carpet that frames the taut carpet of the blue middle area. You can see the mosaic floor of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, with an edge of black and white bands, of the second style. 77 N40510

170. Biclinio (91): from the upper area of this room come the paintings now in the Museo Naz. of Naples (Inv. 8535 and Inv. Rom. DCCLXXXV) detached, from one of the short walls. In fact, one notices the absence of one of the vertical sides of the large red border with stretched garlands, which frames the picture with the Nilotic landscape (ducks among marsh plants).
171. Biclinio (91): upper area. The other painting, symmetrical of the previous one (Inv. Rom. DCOCLXXXV) with a similar subject, Nilotic landscape, but in a worse state of preservation.

172. Tablinum (92): very little remains in situ of the N wall, but enough to recognize with certainty the provenance from this room of several pieces detached in the Bourbon era, and now in the Museo Naz. of Naples. On a low black plinth with plants, in the center of the red middle area, a stretched yellow carpet is arranged, bordered by garlands along the edges. On the sides are red panels, with carpet edges with two parallel lines with squares detached in 1755. Almost nothing remains of the compartments that separated the panels.

173. Tablinum (92), N wall, section O: part of the compartment with a white background with an aedicule with garlands, crossed by a candelabrum on a black background, is now in the Museo Naz. of Naples (Inv. 8585).

174. 'Tablino (92), N wall, section E: the compartment symmetrical to the previous one, in which part of the central stretched carpet can be better distinguished (now in the Museo Naz. in Naples, Inv. 8579); cf. also fig. 177.  AFSN D107733

175. Tablinum (92), N wall: from the carpet stretched in the centre of the middle area comes the couple in flight (now Museo Naz. di Napoli, Inv. 9137), on a yellow background, rather poorly preserved. AFSN D112306

176. Tablinum (92), wall E: black plinth with plants, completely illegible. The middle area, due to the presence of the large window open onto the hortus, has a simplified scheme with red panels with a high yellow border, a small picture (?) removed in the Bourbon era and carpet edges with two parallel lines, of which the guide lines engraved in the still fresh plaster are clearly evident.

182. Atrium (93): view from the SW, when the restoration was completed, with the reconstruction of the upper parts, the roofs and the impluvium of white marble.

The tone of the background color is rather darkened, but the details of the coffered ceiling with a hanging Okeanos mask and the thin reeds ending in palmettes, which frame it, indistinguishable in situ, are clearly legible in the photograph.

Above the panels is a frieze with low metal candelabra supporting garlands. Yellow upper area with hanging architecture and garlands. In the center you can read the collection for a painting (?).

1. Garden (1), N-W section: view from the S when the excavation is completed. The photo records the damage caused to the disturbed S-E section of the summer triclinium: half of the pluteus that was at the base of the pergola, a column, the steps on which to climb to the roof of the niche with a fountain S are missing. The damage was probably done to extract the lead from the fistula and the water tanks of the jets. In fact, even the statuettes that served as a cast are missing. The masonry columns are covered with green plaster. The plaster residues and niches and windows in the perimeter walls belong to the demolished house, whose limit E is given by the joint in the frame work of the wall N visible at the height of the O side of the fountain niche N. The door (buffered) of this house, with jambs of parallelepiped blocks of Sarnense limestone, can be glimpsed behind the worker. In the N-W corner there is a large rectangular tank for watering plants in the garden. Excavation photo 1954.

2. Garden (1), niche with fountain N, S front and E. visible against the back wall the podium of the staircase to climb to the roof. The S façade, in which an apse is obtained, is entirely covered with colored glass mosaic, with the use of shells (cardium edile) to indicate the architectural partitions and large shells (murex brandaris) to highlight the base, center and summit. The whole is imagined as emerging from a cave: the resulting space above the triangular tympanum is covered with fragments of Sarno limestone in order to suggest a rocky wall. The illusion is maintained in the garden painting on the E side, the upper edge of which is frescoed with a row of stalactites. This convention is a constant in Roman painted gardens, starting with the most famous one of the Villa di Livia in Primaporta. Excavation photo 1954. AFS D3514

3. Garden (1), niche fountain N: view from above. The square recess in the roof for housing the lead water tank was again filled with lapilli for conservation reasons. The excavation photo shows the basin of the basin painted green. The monopodium has a circular recess for housing the /abrum. You can see the wall frame and the frieze with duck and fish at the base of the mosaic apse. The pilasters with a blue background on the front are adorned with a motif of overlapping ellipses: a stylization of an acanthus tuft from which two intersecting stems rise, as for example in the pilasters of the so-called furgatorium (F) of the Temple of Isis (VIII 7, 28). The resulting space between them is frescoed with red crowns hanging with a string from the top of the counter. These are the symposiast's crowns, which the participants wore on their heads and/or around their necks during meals, as a sign of devotion to Dionysus.  The white top of the base of the pergola next to the head of the counter N is frescoed with a garland stretched horizontally. The cubic podium in the center of the beds is pierced by a pipe for the water jet which, made operational, prevented it from being used as a canteen.  AFS A111]1 (formerly A8262)

The gush does not disturb the body of water, which makes the shadow of the two doves perched on the edge. Behind them, in the axis of the composition, there is a palm tree with dates falling symmetrically. The garden is full of shrubs. The pairs of straws of which the gate is made are tied by a string knotted in a cross at each intersection of two pairs.

11. Garden (1), niche with fountain N, side E, detail: heron behind. Horizontal beatings are seen so well thanks to the grazing light.

1. Façade, reconstructive view with painted inscriptions, the canopy and the windows on the second floor.

2. Façade, section W, to the left of the door, on which are painted announcements of games and inscriptions of electoral propaganda, collapsed with the wall that served as a support following the bombing of September 1943. The lower part of the façade bears a simple geometric decoration with black panels, which have been partly faded in order to be able to paint other inscriptions.

4. Façade, in which the large portal opens adorned with simple stucco pilasters and cubic capitals dating back to the Republican age. The house was accessed by two steps and a slightly uphill vestibule, from which one could read the overall effect of the architectural and decorative layout, closed by the backdrop in imitation of polychrome marbles of the summer triclinium.

6. Room (d), wall N. The room has been interpreted as a winter triclinium, and the black monochrome background of its walls - also recommended by Vitruvius (VII 4, 4) because it was not ruined by the soot of lamps and hearths - is compared to other rooms with the same function. The monochrome of the environment was accentuated by the papier-mâché floor. The decoration is extremely simple, characterized by a geometric plinth and a middle area that superimposes a light and transparent aedicule on the simple panel scheme. The structure of the middle area continues, still lightened, in the upper area, in the center of which there is also a sort of prospective aedicule. In the decorative arrangement of the room, the presence of figurative paintings has been dispensed with and simple vignettes with animals or other decorative elements appear in the center of the individual fields.
7. Room (d), N wall, section E. Detail of the vignette with a parrot in flight in the centre of the side panel. Last phase of the III style, II B.
8. Room (d), wall E, section N. Black geometric plinth, middle area with black panels divided by a thin candelabrum, upper black area. III style, phase II B.

9. Room (d), wall E, section N, upper area. The low white frieze with lotuses, present between the middle and upper areas, and the slender candelabrum adorned with floral motifs, are typical of the final phase of the III style. III style, phase II B.
10. Room (d), wall E, section S. In the photo you can see the black geometric plinth, surmounted by the central aedicule and the side panels of the middle area.

55. Exedra (y): floor, S section seen from N: the black-and-white mosaic threshold reflects a coffered beam, a typical ornament of ceilings and mosaics of the late Republican period. The two square coffers in the center are highlighted by a strip of squares placed side by side: the one on the left is highlighted by a frame with rectangular shelves, as well as by the diagonals; the one on the right has an ivy leaf, which appears in the center of a circular frame with triangles. The two rectangular side coffers contain a rhombus, the sides of which are marked by a strip of black tiles placed at each corner. The S side of the threshold is covered by a (modern?) rise. For Beyen (Beyen II, p. 203, note 3), the entrance has been narrowed, so that the threshold of the exedra would be cut off by pillar O in opus listatum. There are, however, no visible traces of such an adaptation; the only irregularity that can be ascertained is, if anything, an asymmetry due to the absence of two rows of white tesserae in the E margin of the threshold, which is certainly not cut: pillar E is in republican opus incertum.

63a-b-c. Exedra (y), wall E. The central painting depicts a large and high pink circular base in a wooded landscape, with a golden statue of Dionysus (Moormann: Ariadne) seated in a relaxed pose, the left armpit resting on the tambourine, the right raised above the head holding a kanthàros. He is watched by the panther behind, which jumps beside him. The landscape is illuminated from the right as if the light came from the door in the S. wall (The graphic rendering is from Mau). The architecture depicted illusionistically on the side walls of the exedra seems to be made of a wooden frame painted with a figurative painting inserted in the center of the wall, flanked by niches with a cinnabar red background with statues on a base (cf. Vitruvius, signorum megalographiam et deorum simulacra: De Arch., 7.5.1). The central painting is sheltered by an aedicule with columns with green and white bipartite scales (as if covered with mosaic). The bases of the columns and the leaves leate at half height around the usto are purple and pink, the capitals are of gilded bronze. The yellow forepart on which the columns stand is adorned with a black frieze with pateras alternating with plant tufts, painted as if they were made of gilded bronze. Against the background of the blue sky closed outside the partition of the central painting, a red pelta hangs in the center of the green epistyle also adorned with patera alternating with metal plant tufts. The purple space above the side niches belongs within the room. The tympanum of the aedicule is crowned by plant stems (pro fastigiis appagineculi: Vitr., ibid.) with a glass crater flanked by gilded bronze cupids acting as a central acrotery, and two white winged Amazons with pòlos as lateral acroteria. The Amazons themselves act as a caryatid to the upper epistyle supported by the gilded capitals of the green corner pillars: an effort that is difficult to understand for the eye that does not abstract from the well-differentiated depths of the architectural framework.

The two levels correspond, perhaps, to the ancient subdivision between the vestibule open to the public, and the fauces closed on the street side. The continuity of the frescoed plaster in the third style on the N wall attests that, at least in the imperial era, the room was no longer divided into two parts.

4. Vestibule (a), atrium (b): N-W section with the base of the lararium covered with marble slabs, resting on the N-W corner of the atrium. The base of the lararium and that of the safe, the remains of which are visible between the two doors in the N wall, are placed on the black mosaic of the atrium. The safe was removed during the last days of Pompeii or, as is more likely, from the usual tunnels that penetrated the house by drilling holes in the cubicles (c), (d), (g), in the alae (e) and (h), in the tablinum (i), which also removed the marble covering of the impluvium: which at the time of the excavation was "covered with stucco" (Mau BdI 1876,  p. 150), to say that the bedding layer of the marble slabs was uncovered.

5. Vestibule (a), fauces seen from the W: marble threshold, mosaic of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with respect to the walls, with a black border along the threshold of the vestibule and another black border that delimits the threshold towards the atrium, adorned with L-shaped motifs. The marble slab preserved at the N-E end of the fauces is the base of the door jamb between the fauces and the atrium. The silhouette of the crouching guard dog, executed in black tesserae with the eye and the three stripes on the belly of red tesserae, is located in the axis of the entrance. The fine module of the mosaic (100 cm? = 130 tesserae) indicates its quality, confirming - together with the siIhouette technique - the dating to the Augustan era that can be deduced from the fresco in the third style resting on the edge of the mosaic.

6. Atrium (b), lararium; detail of the decoration of the S side of the base of the aedicule, with the frieze depicting the buildings of the Civic Forum of Pompeii, while they are collapsing as a result of the earthquake of 62 AD.

7. Atrium (b), N section with black mosaic floor enlivened by a regular pattern of colored marble tiles. The edge of the impluvium is marked by a two-strand braid bordering a geometric black and white mosaic motif that imitates a design of opus sectile slabs, of four rectangular tiles arranged around a square slab. The rosettes in the corners of the mosaic border are of Hellenistic tradition. The fresco in the third style that is preserved between the cubicle door (d) and the wing (e), includes a black plinth; under the red middle area with a painting (which vanished already at the time of discovery) figurines two theatrical actors "with long robes who seem to wear masks, and of which the one on the right is seated, the other standing" (Mau BdI 1876, p. 164).

8. Atrium (b), S wall, section O, detail: green plinth, black plinth with yellow picture depicting a competitive vase with palm branch; black predella with a crouching sphinx seen from the front who, on the outstretched wings, holds a yellow box containing three theatrical masks. The box is flanked by oblique thyrsi. The cream-coloured upper frame of the predella is adorned with a series of lotus flowers (see fig. 9). The decoration has now disappeared, regardless of the black background. Graphic restitution from MauW.
9. Atrium (b), S wall, section O, middle area, black predella, detail: the cream-coloured upper frame adorned with lotus flowers. Graphic rendering by Mau W.
10. Atrium (b), S wall, O section, middle area, black predella, detail: cantaro hanging obliquely from a thyrsus under plant scrolls. Graphic restitution from MauW.  from Mau W, tav. XVIIIi

11. Wing (e), N wall, central section, middle area, detail: the upper left corner of the central aedicule with a white background with vine shoots with bunches of grapes vertically, garland stretched diagonally, and horizontal thyrsus. The epistyle is adorned with shells and a Dionysian protome with volutes. The Ionic column is wrapped in meandering collars and battlements. Graphic rendering by Mau W.

12. Wing (e): threshold towards the atrium, in white mosaic with motifs drawn with a row of black tesserae: a concave winged square flanked by peltes, circumscribed blades and lotuses stylized according to the taste of the III style. The tile on the left that interrupts the design of the O end of the mosaic is, perhaps, a post-seismic restoration.  79 N48447

13. Atrium (b), side E, tablinum (i). In the photo that dates back to the twenties and thirties, the mosaic of the atrium is still intact. Originally the tablinum was flanked by corridors, so that customers and servants could circulate without crossing it. In the imperial era, for obvious reasons of space, the S-shaped corridor of the tablinum was abolished to be absorbed by the triclinium (u) on the peristyle, while the wooden door of the former corridor was not touched: the illusion of space remained, symmetry - fundamental in Roman architecture according to Vitruvius (De Arch., I.2.3-4) - was saved, and the needs of space were honored. The door compartment itself is closed with a very irregular masonry on the triclinium side (u), and the wall on that side frescoed in the III style. Evidently, at least three reception rooms were needed: the triclinium (m), (u), and the exedra (0).

14. Atrium (b), section S-E between the tablinum (i) and the walled door of the triclinium (u). The inscription GENIO L NOSTRI!/ FELIX L (CIL X 860) engraved on Cipollino's herm, bears the dedication of the freedman Felix to the Genius of Lucio, 'our master'. It was, probably, a portrait (posthumous?) of the patron offered by the slave who had been tampered with (by will?). The hole in the center of the herm is for the attachment of the bronze phallus.  79 N48551

15. Wing (h): black-and-white mosaic threshold with ivy shoots rising from a chalice, depicted in the centre. The allusion to the Dionysian cult present in the threshold can also be seen in the ornaments of the plinth and in the theatrical paintings of the atrium and tablinum. DAIR 41.280

16. Cubicle (d), S wall with door. The decoration of the upper area is still that of the construction phase of the house: a small floor surmounted by kyma and a stucco dentils cornice, of the first style (II-early first century BC). The protruding frames stopped at a certain distance from the doorway, so as not to be damaged by the leaves. The rest of the wall, worn out by use, is replastered in the last period of Pompeii: with a pink plinth sprinkled with yellow and red with faux granite, and a white middle area articulated by a border of carpet in semicircles.
17. Cubicle (d), S wall, section O, upper area, detail: carpet border (IV style); top surmounted by kyma and stucco dentilled frame. I style.

18. Atrium (b). The view from the E, from the center of the tablinum (i), well illustrates the symmetrical layout of the Samnite house, with slender doors that taper upwards. A hierarchy between the rooms of the atrium district was obtained by means of differentiated depths: greater in the rooms on the N side, less in those on the S side, a circumstance perceptible to the users of the atrium only because of the greater depth of the wing (e) compared to that of the wing (h).

19. Tablinum (i): view from the W, from the atrium through the tablinum in the peristyle. The doors of the tablinum were made of wood, panels supported by the marble plinth. The raised threshold, covered with marble between tablinum and peristyle, is provided with two square recesses for gangheroes. The tunnels have passed into the tablinum through the high hole in the N wall, in correspondence with a smaller one in the S wall. The pillars on the peristyle side are made of brick. The section of the upper area that was painted above the passage to the peristyle (see fig. 37), is no longer in situ.

20. Tablinum (i): floor, central section of the black and white mosaic with a carpet of dodecagons laced with a rosette in the centre. The motif reflects a pattern used for ceilings, as evidenced for example by the carved marble ceilings of the temple of the Divus Hadrian in Piazza di Pietra in Rome. The mosaic modulus is identical to that applied in the fauces (100 cm? = 130 tesserae).
21. Tablinum (i), section O: black-and-white mosaic threshold depicting a coffered beam, arranged in stars of eight rhombuses.

22. Tablinum (i), wall N. The gaps left by the three paintings removed immediately after the excavation, by the hole made by the tunnels and by the partial collapse of the plinth, have been integrated with modern plaster. The hole in the tunnels also appears on the other side of the wall, in the corridor (k). Previously, integration was limited to the two side panels and the plinth (see Fig. 13).

23. Tablinum (i), wall N. Central painting depicting Iphigenia and handmaids in the pronaos of the temple of Artemis in Tauris, in front of Orestes and Pylades (whose figures were destroyed due to the hole in the wall). Detached after the excavation in 1876, the painting is now in the National Museum. of Naples (inv. 111439).

24. Tablinum (i), wall N. Side painting depicting a female bust and a Satyr or Satyress: the female figure facing right (in the center of the wall?) wears a diadem with gold thread, a green veil, earrings, a pendant necklace, a chain on her chest, a bracelet with a green stone on her right forearm and an arm. 1, 23.26
